source_refs.note: Book p. 12: 1.5 Four Fourth Roots of Unity

blocks.text: A fourth root of unity is a number whose fourth power is 1. Let \(x\) be a fourth root of unity. Then

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: \(x^{4} - 1 = (x^{2})^{2} - 1^{2}\) is a difference of two squares, so it factors as \((x^{2} - 1)(x^{2} + 1)\). The product is zero, so one of the factors is zero.
Hence the four fourth roots of unity are: \(1, -1, i, -i\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Check each one: \(1^{4} = 1\), \((-1)^{4} = 1\), \(i^{4} = (i^{2})^{2} = (-1)^{2} = 1\), \((-i)^{4} = (i^{2})^{2} = 1\). Two of the roots are real (\(\pm1\)) and two are imaginary (\(\pm i\)). This agrees with the Fundamental theorem of algebra: \(x^{4} = 1\) has degree 4, so exactly four roots.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Fourth roots of unity are the roots of \(x^{4} = 1\): \(1, -1, i, -i\).
2. They come from \((x^{2} - 1)(x^{2} + 1) = 0\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Stopping at \(x = \pm1\): the factor \(x^{2} + 1 = 0\) gives two more roots, \(\pm i\).
2. Writing \(\sqrt{-1} = -1\): it is \(i\).
